h1: What do the Different Colors of the Bentley Logo Represent?

contentBlocks.text: Ever walked past a Bentley on the street or wandered a car show and caught their winged badges? Bet you’ve noticed they don’t all match up. Every emblem’s got those legendary wings, obviously—but get up close to the middle circular core, and the background hues vary dramatically. Some carry green centers, some black, while red and blue iterations also appear across vintage and modern models.

Most casual onlookers assume these color variations are just random cosmetic flourishes or costly custom add-ons. The truth holds far deeper historical and mechanical context. Seasoned Bentley enthusiasts can instantly read a car’s lineage, powertrain specification and positioning simply by glancing at that central circle. Each shade pays homage to a distinct chapter of the brand’s century-long legacy, acting as a quick visual decoder for what lies under the hood.
So what do these distinct badge center colors truly stand for? Are they purely decorative, or does every tone carry a piece of Bentley’s origin story?
Let’s break down the layered, evolving color coding system behind the iconic winged Bentley emblem.
The "Flying B" Hood Ornament

The retractable "Flying B" hood mascot exists entirely separate from the grille-mounted Winged B badge’s color coding—this is critical to avoid confusion. It is more than just a decorative hood piece; it is an iconic automotive status symbol rooted in Bentley’s 1920s racing heritage. When you spotted this polished 'B' perched atop an 8 Litre’s bonnet, it immediately signaled unrivaled road dominance. Over generations, it has become the signature finishing touch for flagship nameplates including the Mulsanne, Azure and Arnage, a constant reminder that supreme luxury does not require muted performance.
The 2006 Comeback

After decades of discontinuation due to pedestrian safety regulations, the Flying B made its fully engineered return in 2006. Bentley’s engineers integrated a fully retractable mechanical mechanism: it retracts flush into the hood upon impact to meet global safety standards, while delivering dramatic theatrical flair as it rises automatically when the vehicle ignites.
The 2019 Centenary Redesign

To mark Bentley’s 100th anniversary, designer Hoe Young Hwang reimagined the mascot with an owl as its core inspiration—an animal calm and composed at rest, yet ferociously swift when striking. This contrast of serene elegance and ferocious power mirrors the dual personality of the modern Flying Spur: a refined mobile boardroom until the driver hits full throttle.
Mulliner Custom Finishes

Standard factory Flying B ornaments ship in polished silver chrome, but Mulliner’s bespoke division offers fully personalized alternatives for collectors. Dark tinted, matte tungsten, translucent illuminated crystal, and solid 24k gold finishes are all available as exclusive upgrades. These custom hood ornaments are purely aesthetic choices, with no link to the vehicle’s engine or trim level.
The "Winged B" Grille Badge (Central Circle Color Coding)

The wide-spread Winged B grille badge holds the brand’s core visual language, drafted originally by designer F. Gordon Crosby. The outstretched wings pay tribute to W.O. Bentley’s early career designing World War One aircraft engines, symbolizing unbridled speed and aerodynamic motion. As an anti-counterfeiting feature, Crosby intentionally designed each wing to carry a different number of feather segments.

Crucially, the solid color filling the badge’s central roundel operates as a tiered classification system that has shifted across three major eras of Bentley production: the 1920s vintage Label models, the 1990s Rolls-Royce-owned Arnage/Continental generation, and the modern post-2003 Volkswagen Group lineup. Below is the accurate breakdown for each shade:
1. Black Roundel Badge: Flagship Performance Identity
A common misconception is that black-centered emblems serve as the standard factory fitment for regular production cars—this is incorrect. Black roundels carry two distinct applications today:

Factory-native black badging (W12 / Speed / Black Edition models): All vehicles fitted with the 6.0L twin-turbo W12 engine, alongside Speed and Black Edition performance variants, roll off the production line with an original black core badge. This color exclusively signifies top-tier horsepower, sport-tuned chassis hardware and the brand’s peak performance hierarchy, commanding a significant price premium over standard V8 models.

After-fit black badging via Blackline Specification: Standard 4.0L V8 models ship with red roundels from the factory, but buyers may opt for the Blackline cosmetic package, which swaps the red core for a black badge alongside fully blacked-out exterior chrome trim. This is a visual modification only; the vehicle retains its standard V8 powertrain with no mechanical upgrades.

Across 1990s classic Bentleys including the Continental T, black roundels were also factory standard for the range’s most powerful grand tourers, cementing the long-standing brand association between black badges and uncompromised performance.
2. Red Roundel Badge: The Modern Standard V8 & Original Racing Bloodline

Contrary to the myth that all pre-1924 Bentleys carried red badges, the 1920s 3 Litre lineup featured three concurrent vintage Label grades: Blue Label (base comfort tourer), Red Label (high-output sport chassis), and Green Label (limited-production racing supercar). Red was reserved for the brand’s original sport-focused grand tourers, establishing its foundational racing heritage.

For all modern post-2003 standard production vehicles fitted with the 4.0L twin-turbo V8 engine—including the Flying Spur V8, Continental GT V8 and Bentayga V8—the red roundel is the factory default fitment with no optional powertrain upgrades attached. These V8 models represent Bentley’s balanced, daily-drivable mainstream lineup, delivering a harmonious blend of luxury, practicality and accessible performance. Red remains the marker of Bentley’s core volume grand tourer formula, tracing its lineage back to the marque’s earliest racing roots.
3. Green Roundel Badge: Vintage Motorsport Heritage, Modern Custom Only

Green draws its iconic meaning from British Racing Green and the legendary Le Mans victories claimed by the Bentley Boys in the 1920s. The ultra-rare 1920s Green Label 3 Litre represented the brand’s original racing flagship.

In the 1990s Arnage lineup, green roundels were factory fitted exclusively to the entry-level Arnage Green Label variant, a lower-powered model powered by a BMW-sourced V8 engine. No new modern Bentley leaves the factory with a green center badge today; green roundels are only available as a Mulliner bespoke custom finish for clients seeking a vintage motorsport tribute, with no bearing on the car’s performance tier. They remain a beloved nod to Bentley’s unrivaled Le Mans racing legacy.
4. Blue Roundel Badge: Vintage Azure Convertible Exclusive, Bespoke Retro Option

Blue-centered badges were never assigned to ultra-luxury one-off bespoke commissions as a universal marker of exclusivity. Historically, blue roundels were factory-exclusive to the Azure convertible range produced throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, crafted to symbolize laid-back, open-top cruising luxury focused on relaxed long-distance comfort.

For contemporary 2003-onwards vehicles, blue roundels are no longer a factory standard fitment. They can only be specified via Mulliner’s bespoke division as a retro styling choice for any V8 or W12 model. A blue core badge does not signify a top-tier, one-of-one custom build—fully individualized Mulliner commissions can be ordered with red, black, green or blue roundels interchangeably based purely on client aesthetic preference.
5. Special Edition: The Centenary Gold Badge (1919–2019)

To celebrate Bentley’s 100th anniversary of manufacturing, every vehicle built during the 2019 centenary production year received a unique commemorative Winged B badge. This special emblem features a polished "Centenary Gold" metallic finish, flanked by the founding year 1919 and centenary year 2019 on either side of the central 'B'. It honors F. Gordon Crosby’s original 1919 winged design, bridging a century of racing heritage and modern ultra-luxury engineering.
The Verdict: Decoding the Winged B Roundel Color Code

Next time you spot a Bentley, pause to examine its grille badge’s central circle. This emblem is far more than corporate branding—it acts as a concise visual summary of the car’s engineering identity and brand positioning. Bentley’s roundel color system bridges its competitive racing origins and modern bespoke luxury, with clear, era-dependent rules:

Black Core Badge: Two distinct definitions. Factory-native black identifies flagship W12 and Speed high-performance models with upgraded mechanical hardware. Blackline cosmetic package black badges appear on standard V8 vehicles as a purely visual sporty styling upgrade, with no powertrain changes. Across all generations, black remains tied to peak performance potential.

Red Core Badge: The factory standard fitment for all modern 4.0L V8 grand tourers, Bentley’s balanced daily-driving volume model. It honors the marque’s 1920s sport-label racing origins, representing the accessible, well-rounded core of the brand’s lineup.

Green Core Badge: A tribute to the Bentley Boys’ historic Le Mans racing triumphs. No longer factory standard on new cars; only offered via Mulliner custom orders as a retro heritage styling accent. Historically used for both 1920s racing supercars and the 1990s Arnage entry-level model.

Blue Core Badge: Originally factory-exclusive to the vintage Azure soft-top convertible range, symbolizing leisurely open-air cruising comfort. Today only available as a Mulliner retro custom finish for any model, with no link to exclusive one-off bespoke build hierarchy.

Long before the engine ignites and roars, the winged badge’s central color already communicates the vehicle’s intended purpose and heritage. It is a subtle, metallic secret language shared between Bentley and its most knowledgeable enthusiasts. The next time you pass a Bentley on the road, take a closer look at its tiny colored core—you will discover far more layered history and intentional engineering coding than you might expect.
